variable (R : Type u) [CommRing R] [Algebra k R]

/-- **Base change of properness to an arbitrary test ring**: the second projection of
`C ⊗ Spec R` is proper, for every commutative `k`-algebra `R` — the general-`R` form of
`Curve/BaseChangeInstances.instIsProperSndLeft` (which is keyed on field extensions).
This is the DDR-4 support-tube licence over the `Z(♦)`-chart rings `R_Z`. -/
instance instIsProperRelSndLeft : IsProper (snd C (overSpec k R)).left :=
  MorphismProperty.of_isPullback (P := @IsProper)
    (Over.isPullback_left C (overSpec k R)) inferInstance

/-- The properness instance, keyed on the `relCurve C R ↘ Spec R` spelling installed by
`relCurve.instOver` (definitionally the second projection). In particular
`UniversallyClosed (relCurve C R ↘ Spec R)` fires by resolution, which is what
`Scheme.LocalEquations.exists_supportTube` consumes. -/
instance instIsProperRelCurveHom :
    IsProper ((relCurve C R) ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of R)) :=
  inferInstanceAs (IsProper (snd C (overSpec k R)).left)

/-- Acceptance smoke test: the support tube applies to the relative curve over an
arbitrary test ring with the universally-closed instance found by resolution. -/

import AlgebraicJacobian.Picard.DivSchemeCertZarPointwise
import AlgebraicJacobian.Picard.SupportTubeFinite

/-!
# The support tube in `Away`-chart form

The pointwise certificate gate (`DivSchemeCertZarPointwise.lean`) asks, at each base prime
`p`, for an element `r ∉ p` such that the pulled system is certified over
`Localization.Away r`.  The support tube (`Scheme.LocalEquations.exists_supportTube`)
delivers piece isolation over an *abstract* Zariski neighbourhood `V` of `p`.  This file
refines that neighbourhood to a basic open — the shape `Localization.Away` needs — and
records the resulting statement.

The refinement is the standard fact that basic opens form a topological basis of
`Spec R` (`PrimeSpectrum.isBasis_basic_opens`); the content is only that the tube's
conclusion is monotone in the neighbourhood, so shrinking `V` to a basic open inside it
preserves support isolation.

## Main declarations

* `AlgebraicGeometry.Scheme.LocalEquations.exists_basicOpen_supportTube` — the tube with a
  basic-open neighbourhood: an `r ∉ p` whose basic open isolates the support inside `U`.
* `AlgebraicGeometry.exists_notMem_supportLocus_subset_of_fibre` — the same for the
  relative curve over a test ring, with the properness licence supplied.
-/

set_option autoImplicit false
set_option maxSynthPendingDepth 3

universe u

open CategoryTheory Limits TopologicalSpace Opposite

namespace AlgebraicGeometry

attribute [local instance] Scheme.overModule Scheme.overSectionsAlgebra

namespace Scheme.LocalEquations

variable {X : Scheme.{u}} {R : Type u} [CommRing R] (d : X.LocalEquations)

/-- **The support tube with a basic-open neighbourhood.** If the support fibre over a base
prime `p` lies inside an open `U`, then some `r ∉ p` has its whole basic-open preimage's
support inside `U`.

The tube produces an abstract neighbourhood; basic opens are a basis of `Spec R`
(`PrimeSpectrum.isBasis_basic_opens`), so shrinking to a basic open inside it keeps the
conclusion by monotonicity of the preimage. This is the form the `Localization.Away`
charts of `IsLocallyCertified` consume. -/
theorem exists_basicOpen_supportTube (f : X ⟶ Spec (CommRingCat.of R))
    [UniversallyClosed f] {U : Set X} (hU : IsOpen U) {p : PrimeSpectrum R}
    (hfib : f.base ⁻¹' {(p : Spec (CommRingCat.of R))} ∩ d.supportLocus ⊆ U) :
    ∃ r : R, r ∉ p.asIdeal ∧
      f.base ⁻¹' ((PrimeSpectrum.basicOpen r : Opens (PrimeSpectrum R)) :
          Set (Spec (CommRingCat.of R))) ∩ d.supportLocus ⊆ U := by
  obtain ⟨V, hpV, hV⟩ := d.exists_supportTube f hU hfib
  -- refine `V` to a basic open around `p`
  obtain ⟨W, ⟨r, rfl⟩, hpW, hWV⟩ :=
    PrimeSpectrum.isBasis_basic_opens.exists_subset_of_mem_open (a := p)
      (by exact hpV) V.isOpen
  refine ⟨r, by simpa only [PrimeSpectrum.mem_basicOpen] using hpW, ?_⟩
  exact fun x hx => hV ⟨hWV hx.1, hx.2⟩

end Scheme.LocalEquations

/-! ## The relative-curve form -/

section RelCurve

variable {k : Type u} [Field k] (C : Over (Spec (.of k))) [IsProper C.hom]
variable (R : Type u) [CommRing R] [Algebra k R]

/-- **The relative-curve support tube, basic-open form.** For a local-equation system on
the relative curve over a test ring, fibrewise containment of the support in an open `U`
at a prime `p` gives an `r ∉ p` isolating the support over the basic open of `r`.

The properness licence is `instIsProperRelCurveHom`; `UniversallyClosed` fires by
resolution. -/
theorem exists_notMem_supportLocus_subset_of_fibre
    (d : (relCurve C R).LocalEquations) {U : Set (relCurve C R)} (hU : IsOpen U)
    {p : PrimeSpectrum R}
    (hfib : ((relCurve C R) ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of R)).base ⁻¹'
        {(p : Spec (CommRingCat.of R))} ∩ d.supportLocus ⊆ U) :
    ∃ r : R, r ∉ p.asIdeal ∧
      ((relCurve C R) ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of R)).base ⁻¹'
          ((PrimeSpectrum.basicOpen r : Opens (PrimeSpectrum R)) :
            Set (Spec (CommRingCat.of R))) ∩ d.supportLocus ⊆ U :=
  d.exists_basicOpen_supportTube _ hU hfib

end RelCurve

end AlgebraicGeometry

11	
12	## You are a team; the workspace is where teams collaborate
13	
14	Think of your session as **one team**: you (the lead) plus the subagents you
15	spawn as your **workers**, with the tools and skills available to you. A
16	`horizon run` is your team working through its task. Other runs are **other
17	teams** working in parallel on the *same shared workspace* — one Lean project set,

29	  other teams just produced (skill: `project-git`).

36	## Orient (pull state, don't assume it)

118	This session runs to completion and is **not resumed** — you will not be re-invoked
119	when a background job finishes. So **run work in the foreground and block on it**

1	---
2	name: horizon-inbox
3	description: Read and act on the Archon Horizon inbox — list/filter items, understand labels/kinds, comment, archive, create; per-team ownership and read-state; and message other projects or teams via the `horizon inbox` CLI.
4	---
5	
6	The inbox is the durable channel between the human, agent sessions (present and
7	future), and other projects. Act on it through the CLI; never edit inbox files
8	by hand. Prefer `--json` whenever reading command output for exact ids or
9	fields.
10	
11	## Read
12	
13	- `horizon inbox list` — read the inbox. Use `--json` when you need exact ids,
14	  labels, scope, author, audience, timestamps, or comments. Use the list filters
15	  to narrow without losing the overview: `--to horizon`, `--to human`,
16	  `--project P`, repeated `--kind K`, repeated `--label L`,
17	  `--status open`, `--query TEXT`, `--limit N`, and `--comments N`.
18	- Every inbox command evaluates the full local working set, even when `list` is
19	  filtered. Treat its advisory warnings as a prompt to review duplicates, stale
20	  memories, and consumed notices. The CLI never archives automatically because
21	  only the working agent can decide what is resolved; that agent must make an
22	  explicit cleanup pass before its final report.
23	- Labels are the release gate. Local inbox items default to `agent-ready`, which
24	  means they are visible to agents at run boundaries. Keep that default for
25	  machine-addressed work, and usually keep it for human-addressed notices too:
26	  it helps later agents see that the human has already been notified and avoids
27	  duplicate reports. Use `not-ready`, `rejected`, or no labels only when there is
28	  a concrete reason agents should not see or act on the item yet.
29	- Audience says who should read the item: empty/general, `horizon`, `human`,
30	  `project:<name>`, or a **direct message** to another team: `task:<id>` /
31	  `run:<id>` (older items may carry the legacy `ground` audience).
32	  Scope/project says what the item is about.
33	- Horizon reads general items, items addressed to `horizon`, items addressed
34	  to its project, and DMs addressed to its own task/run. It should ignore other
35	  projects' and other teams' addressed items.
36	- Kinds: `hint` (normal guidance), `issue` (problem to fix/report),
37	  `protection` (standing constraint / soft freeze), `info` (a notice for the
38	  human — something you did or noticed they should know, e.g. a renamed project
39	  or an important change; purely informational, never affects what runs),
40	  `memory` (durable agent note or dead end).
41	
42	## Ownership & read-state (your team's inbox)
43	
44	Each running session is a **team**, and the inbox is shared across teams. Two
45	lightweight overlays keep it navigable:
46	
47	- **Ownership** — an item is either *shared with everyone* (the default) or
48	  *owned by one task* (that team's private inbox — e.g. its own memory). Read your
49	  team's inbox with `horizon inbox list --mine` (owned-by-you **plus** shared);
50	  another team's private items don't appear. Own an item to your task with
51	  `horizon inbox add --mine …` (or `--owner <task-id>`), and `horizon inbox own
52	  <id> --mine|--owner <task>|--shared` to move an existing one. Owning your
53	  `--kind memory` notes keeps another team's memory out of your working set.
54	- **Read-state** — read/unread is **per team**, so a shared item several teams see
55	  tracks who has read it. `horizon inbox list --unread` is what *you* have not read
56	  yet; `horizon inbox read <id>` marks it read, and `horizon inbox unread <id>`
57	  puts it back (e.g. you read it but it still needs action). Combine:
58	  `horizon inbox list --mine --unread` is your team's fresh queue — the same signal
59	  the pre-command synchronizer counts for you.
60	
61	The reader/owner id is inferred from your session (your task), so you rarely pass
62	it explicitly.
63	
64	## Act
65	
66	Authorship is automatic: every item and comment you create through the CLI is
67	attributed to your role (normally `horizon`) from the run environment — you do
68	**not** pass `--author` (a stray `--author work-reviewer` is demoted to the
69	`agent` metadata, not used as the author, so the author set stays conventional).
70	If you are a dispatched **subagent**, add `--agent <your-name>` (e.g. `--agent
71	work-reviewer`) to record your identity; it is stored in metadata and shown
72	next to the role in the UI, keeping the author itself a clean role. Items and
73	comments are also auto-tagged with the run/session provenance (a small chip in the
74	UI); you do not pass this yourself.
75	
76	New inbox items use a two-part body:
77	
78	- First paragraph = concise title. Keep it short enough to scan in one UI row
79	  (aim for under ~100 characters); do not put the full explanation here.
80	- Second paragraph and later = non-empty description. Put the evidence, impact,
81	  next action, and relevant ids/files here. The description is **mandatory** — an
82	  item that is only a title is rejected.
83	
84	Write bodies and comments in **Markdown**: the dashboard renders it. Use short
85	paragraphs and `-` bullet lists instead of one wall-of-text paragraph, `**bold**`
86	for the key claim, and backticks for ids, lemma names, files, and code
87	(`` `lem:foo` ``, `` `Foo.lean:42` ``). A long unstructured blob is hard to scan.
88	
89	Do not create an item whose body is only a title. If you need a `[persistent]` or
90	`[temporary]` tag, put it at the start of the title paragraph and keep the rest
91	of that paragraph concise.
92	
93	Before opening a new item, search the open inbox for the same topic using
94	`horizon inbox list --status open --query "key words" --json` and, when relevant,
95	`--project P` / `--to R`. If a live item already covers the same issue, do not
96	open a duplicate: add a comment with the new evidence, or edit the body if the
97	main description is stale. If you discover an open item is obsolete, already
98	solved, consumed, or superseded, add a short comment when the reason is not
99	obvious and then run `horizon inbox archive <id>`.
100	
101	- `horizon inbox comment <id> --body "..."` — progress note on an item (record
102	  what you did; not to ask the human for clarification). Do not write your name
103	  into the comment body; the author is set automatically. Drop a comment at each **key advance**
104	  while you work an item (a milestone reached, a route ruled out, a blocker hit),
105	  not only at the end — these comments are the item's visible progress trail.
106	- **Write comments as mathematics, for a human.** State the key step that
107	  succeeded in human-readable mathematical language (LaTeX for formulas), naming
108	  the result and the idea — e.g. "Proved $H^i(X,\mathcal{F})=0$ for $i>\dim X$ by
109	  reducing to the affine case via Čech cohomology." Mention Lean declaration
110	  names and file paths only as supporting detail; the substance is the maths, not
111	  a code changelog. This applies to comments on **roadmap items and tasks** too:
112	  when a key step lands, record it there in the same mathematical, legible style.
113	- `horizon inbox archive <id>` — soft-delete: keep the item for the record but
114	  hide it from the dashboard by default. Use for stale, superseded, consumed, or
115	  no-longer-key context. Keeping the inbox tidy this way is your job (or the
116	  janitor subagent's) — prune memory/info so they remain small.
117	- `horizon inbox complete <id>` — mark an item resolved only when it records work
118	  you genuinely concluded and want to keep visible outside the archive. Before
119	  completing, add a short **conclusion comment**: first the mathematical
120	  conclusion (what was proved/established, in words + LaTeX), then concise
121	  metadata (runs, approximate LOC, files/declarations involved). A reader should
122	  grasp the result and how it was concluded without opening the logs.
123	- `horizon inbox add --body "Short title\n\nDescription with details and next action." [--to R] [--project P] [--persistent|--temporary] [--agent <name> if a subagent]`
124	  — open a new item.
125	  - `--to` is the recipient: `horizon`, `human`, `project:<name>`, or a direct
126	    message to another team `task:<id>` / `run:<id>`.
127	    Use `--to project:<name>` to message another project (e.g. "I rewrote your
128	    `foo` declaration more cleanly, you may want it"); use `--to task:<id>` to
129	    message a specific running team.
130	  - `--owner <task-id>` / `--mine` keeps the item in one team's inbox instead of
131	    the shared default.
132	  - `--project` says what the item is ABOUT (its subject).
133	  - `--persistent` / `--temporary` just prepend a `[persistent]` / `[temporary]`
134	    tag to the body.
135	  - `--pending` labels the item `not-ready` instead of the default `agent-ready`,
136	    so it stays invisible to agents until a human releases it.
137	- `horizon inbox add --kind memory --to horizon --body "Short memory title\n\nDurable fact, convention, or dead end."` — record a durable
138	  note / dead end. Memory lives in the inbox, so it is rendered in the "Memory"
139	  section and a human can prune it like any other item.
140	- `horizon inbox protect --body "..." [--project P] [--file F] [--declaration D] [--blueprint-node N]`
141	  — add a semantic standing constraint the Horizon agent must respect (a soft freeze),
142	  e.g. "do not change the signature of `Foo.bar`". These render as a
143	  "Protected" section; honour them, including semantic ones. For a target that
144	  must be mechanically blocked before dispatch, the user uses the config-backed
145	  `horizon freeze add <file|declaration|blueprint-node> <target>` command instead.
146	
147	Reading convention: an item tagged `[persistent]` is a standing rule — respect
148	it every round and keep it open while relevant. `[temporary]` (or untagged) is
149	one-shot — archive it once consumed. Items in the "Protected" section are never
150	modified.

end RelCurve

/-! ## No-leak over a shrunken base, from one fibre

The point of the tube in the certificate lane: the no-leak hypothesis that is false
globally becomes *true over the tube*, because the support over the tube is already inside
the piece — so its closure is too, and the fibre clause holds for every base point of the
tube rather than only the one it was checked at. -/

section NoLeakOverTube

variable {k : Type u} [Field k] {C : Over (Spec (.of k))} [IsProper C.hom]
variable {R : Type u} [CommRing R] [Algebra k R]
variable {pi : C.left ⟶ P1 k} [IsAffineHom pi]
variable {d : (relCurve C R).LocalEquations} (A : DivisorAdaptation C R pi d)

/-- **Support containment upgrades to the fibrewise no-leak clause.** If the whole family
support lies in the piece `j`, then over every base point the fibre of the *closure* of the
piece trace stays in the piece: the trace is then all of the support, which is closed.

This is the bridge between what the tube delivers (support containment over a shrunken
base) and what the certificate assembler consumes (the fibrewise clause of
`finite_colength_of_forall_fibre_closure_subset`). -/
theorem forall_fibre_closure_subset_of_supportLocus_subset (j : A.index)
    (hsub : d.supportLocus ⊆ (A.pieces j : Set (relCurve C R))) :
    ∀ s : Spec (CommRingCat.of R),
      ((relCurve C R) ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of R)).base ⁻¹' {s}
          ∩ closure (d.supportLocus ∩ (A.pieces j : Set (relCurve C R)))
        ⊆ (A.pieces j : Set (relCurve C R)) := by
  intro s x hx
  have htrace : d.supportLocus ∩ (A.pieces j : Set (relCurve C R)) = d.supportLocus :=
    Set.inter_eq_left.mpr hsub
  rw [htrace, d.isClosed_supportLocus.closure_eq] at hx
  exact hsub hx.2

/-- The no-leak clause for **every** piece, from containment of the support in each: the
exact `hnoLeak` input of the certificate assemblers
(`DivisorAdaptation.isCertified_of_noLeak_kernel_spanning`,
`ThetaGeneratorSeed.divisorAdaptation_isCertified_of_noLeak_kernel_spanning`). -/
theorem forall_noLeak_of_forall_supportLocus_subset
    (hsub : ∀ j : A.index, d.supportLocus ⊆ (A.pieces j : Set (relCurve C R))) :
    ∀ (j : A.index) (s : Spec (CommRingCat.of R)),
      ((relCurve C R) ↘ Spec (CommRingCat.of R)).base ⁻¹' {s}
          ∩ closure (d.supportLocus ∩ (A.pieces j : Set (relCurve C R)))
        ⊆ (A.pieces j : Set (relCurve C R)) :=
  fun j => A.forall_fibre_closure_subset_of_supportLocus_subset j (hsub j)

end NoLeakOverTube

end AlgebraicGeometry
